questions: Which value problem does each proposal answer, and what assumptions drive the swamping argument?

used_for: Plato's question and the held-fixed comparison
Stability is a capacity to withstand misleading changes
Is value exhausted when the end is absent as well?
The object of evaluation can be larger than one belief

evidence.excerpt: In Plato’s Meno, Socrates raises the question of why knowledge is more valuable than mere true belief.
Mere true belief at this point might be lost, since one might lose all confidence that this is the right way to go.
However, it requires further development to answer the secondary value problem.
The tertiary value problem pertains to why knowledge is qualitatively better than any epistemic standing falling short of knowledge.

The first contemporary wave of work on the value problem largely concerned whether this problem raised a distinctive difficulty for reliabilist accounts of knowledge—i.e., those views which essentially define knowledge as reliably-formed true belief.
In defense of this claim, she offers the analogy of a cup of coffee.

Elsewhere in the literature (e.g., Kvanvig 2003), this problem has been called the “swamping problem”, on account of how the value of true belief ‘swamps’ the value of the true belief being produced in a reliable (i.e., truth-conducive) way.
It’s actually not clear that this is a problem that is specific to reliabilism.
Adam Carter and Benjamin Jarvis (2012) have argued, there are reasons to be suspicious of a key premise driving the swamping argument.

However, as they argue, the Swamping Thesis and the Swamping Thesis Complement, along with other plausible premises, jointly entail the unpalatable conclusion that non-factive epistemic properties—most notably, justification—are never epistemically valuable properties of a belief.
Brown 2012; Davis, & Jäger 2012; Hovarth 2009; Piller 2009).
For example, agent reliabilism (e.g., Greco 1999, 2000) might be thought to be untouched by this sort of argument.

Plausibly, however, one might argue that the reliable traits that make up an agent’s cognitive character have some value independently of the instrumental value they possess in virtue of being reliable—i.e., that they have some final or intrinsic value.

It is not clear what exactly Zagzebski means by this point, but she thinks it shows that even where the reliable process is independently valuable—i.e., independently of its being reliable—it still doesn’t follow that the value of the cause will transfer to add value to the effect.

On this picture, then, we are not to understand knowledge as a state consisting of a known belief, but rather as a state which consists of both the true belief and the source from which that true belief was acquired.

In particular, if the process by which one gained the true belief is an epistemic virtue—a character trait which is both reliable and intrinsically valuable—then this can ensure that the value of the knowing state in this case is more valuable than any corresponding state which simply consisted of a true belief.

Rather than treating the extra value of knowledge over true belief as deriving simply from the agent’s attainment of the target true belief, however, Riggs and Greco instead argue that we should regard the agent’s knowing as the state the agent is in when she is responsible for her true belief.

If one holds that there is only intrinsic and instrumental value, then this conception of value is compelling, since objects with the same intrinsic properties trivially have the same amount of intrinsic value, and they also plausibly have the same amount of instrumental value as well (at least in the same sort of environment).
For criticism of this account of final value, see Bradley (2002).

evidence.excerpt: Nevertheless, his belief is subject to environmental luck in that he is, unbeknownst to him, in barn façade county in which every other barn-shaped object is a barn façade.

evidence.locator: § § 3. Virtue Epistemology and the Value Problem
evidence.excerpt: Robust virtue epistemologists have made a number of salient points regarding this case.

The two usages of the term ‘understanding’ in ordinary language that Kvanvig focuses on—and which he regards as being especially important to epistemology—are when understanding is claimed for some object, such as some subject matter, and when it involves understanding that something is the case.

This requirement entails that understanding is directly factive in the case of propositional understanding and indirectly factive in the case of objectual understanding—i.e., the agent needs to have at least mostly true beliefs about the target subject matter in order to be truly said to have objectual understanding of that subject matter.

evidence.locator: § § 6. Other Accounts of the Value of Knowledge
evidence.excerpt: Moreover, were this agent to use this belief as a premise in her practical reasoning, and so infer that she should throw the ticket away without checking the lottery results in the paper for example, then we would regard her reasoning as problematic.

evidence.locator: § § 6. Other Accounts of the Value of Knowledge
evidence.excerpt: If the agent had formed her true belief by reading the results in a reliable newspaper, for example, then she would count as knowing the target proposition and can then infer that she should throw the ticket away without criticism.
